top_choice_rationale: The optical lattice clock (Katori and Ye) rests on one clear physical idea, a magic-wavelength trap that does not shift the clock transition. Its 10^-18 performance has been checked by direct comparison between independent clocks in several laboratories. It has already produced physics (gravitational redshift over centimetres, bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, clock-based geodesy). The two-name allocation is traceable, and a citation worded around the lattice principle stays clear of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. Twisted bilayer graphene (P001) is a strong second, with a prediction followed by an experiment and broad reproduction, but the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder are still open. I rank it above no award, and I could vote for it.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; his Lund atomic-physics and Hall-lab ties are adjacent to precision-metrology work but do not involve Katori or Ye directly, and he has no apparent connection to the twisted-graphene laureates
